resources.string: What are the standards for milk testing?
What Is the Acidity or pH of Milk?
What is the SNF in milk?
What is A1 and A2 milk?

The COB test is a rapid screening test used to check the freshness and stability of milk. If milk curdles or clots when boiled, it indicates high acidity (due to bacterial spoilage or mastitis), meaning the milk is spoiled and unsuitable for processing.

Standard milk testing involves checking FAT percentage, SNF (Solid Not Fat) content, CLR (Corrected Lactometer Reading) at 29°C temperature, acidity/pH, and checking for adulterants like water, urea, detergent, and starch.

Fresh, raw cow\'s milk typically has a pH between 6.5 and 6.7 (slightly acidic to neutral). An increase in acidity (lower pH) indicates bacterial fermentation and lactic acid production, signaling souring or spoilage.

SNF refers to the total solids in milk excluding butterfat and water. It includes proteins (casein, whey), lactose, and minerals (ash). For cow milk, standard SNF is around 8.5%, and for buffalo milk, it is around 9.0%.

Milk density is measured using a lactometer. Normal cow milk density ranges from 1.028 to 1.030 g/ml, and buffalo milk ranges from 1.030 to 1.032 g/ml. Watering milk decreases density, while skimming increases it.
The primary natural acid in fresh milk is lactic acid (formed when bacteria ferment milk lactose), along with citric acid and free fatty acids.

A1 and A2 refer to two different types of beta-casein protein found in cow\'s milk. A2 milk comes from cows that produce only A2 beta-casein (common in indigenous/desi breeds like Gir, Sahiwal), which many people find easier to digest than A1 milk.
Fat and SNF Standards by Milk Type

Different milk types have standardized composition requirements:
• Cow Milk: 3.5% FAT, 8.5% SNF
• Buffalo Milk: 6.0% FAT, 9.0% SNF
• Toned Milk: 3.0% FAT, 8.5% SNF
• Double Toned Milk: 1.5% FAT, 9.0% SNF
• Standardized Milk: 4.5% FAT, 8.5% SNF

Strict quality parameters ensure milk is safe for consumption and free from harmful adulterants:
• Added Water: Detected via freezing point or lactometer density.
• Urea: Normal range is up to 70 mg/100ml; higher indicates deliberate adulteration.
• Detergent / Soap: Should be completely absent (tested via surface tension or dye tests).
• Starch / Maltodextrin: Added to increase SNF; must be 0% (detected via iodine test).
• Neutralizers (Soda/Formalin): Added to prevent souring; strictly prohibited in raw milk.

Regulatory authorities enforce strict maximum residue limits (MRLs) and contaminant caps to ensure dairy safety:
• Pesticide Residues: Must not exceed 0.01 to 0.05 mg/kg depending on compound type.
• Heavy Metals (Lead/Mercury): Maximum allowable limits are 0.02 mg/kg for lead and 0.001 mg/kg for mercury.
• Aflatoxin M1: Regulated tightly at a maximum cap of 0.5 µg/kg (parts per billion).
• Antibiotic Residues: Zero tolerance; milk containing antibiotic traces is rejected entirely.

Under FSSAI regulations, various dairy products must meet strict compositional standards: • Table Butter: Minimum 80.0\% Milk Fat and maximum 16.0\% moisture. • White Butter: Minimum 76.0\% Milk Fat. • Ghee: Derived exclusively from milk, cream, or butter with specified Reichert value (RV) and moisture limits. • Khoa: Minimum 55.0\% total solids and minimum 30.0\% milk fat on dry matter basis. • Paneer / Chhana: Maximum 60.0\% moisture (Paneer) / 65.0\% moisture (Chhana), with a minimum of 50.0\% fat on a dry matter basis. • Ice Cream / Kulfi: Must meet specific minimum protein, total solids, and milk fat requirements depending on whether it is plain, fruit, or nut-based.
